The following is a summary from an article in "New Scientist" magazine.
In 2010, there will be more than one billion people living on Earth. By mid-century that number could reach three or four times as many - and by then we'll have to find new ways for them all to live together without destroying our planet's resources.
One solution may lie with nanotechnology: tiny machines made up of molecules just tens of atoms wide which can perform tasks ranging from building bridges to cleaning your teeth (see 'Nanotech toothbrush').
But it won't happen overnight; even if scientists manage to build such devices within five years they would take decades before their benefits were felt across society. So what should governments do now?
Firstly, says David Keith at Harvard University, US, who has written about this issue extensively ("Climate Change Policy", MIT Press), politicians need to stop thinking like economists when considering how best to deal with climate change. Economists tend towards short-term solutions because these are easier to measure but long term ones often work better.
For example, while carbon taxes might seem expensive today, over time they become cheaper since emissions fall faster once you've paid for reducing pollution. And although some argue against taxing fossil fuels until renewable energy becomes cheap enough to compete directly, others say doing so encourages innovation into clean technologies sooner rather than later.
Secondly, he suggests focusing efforts not only around cutting greenhouse gas levels quickly through measures including cap-and-trade schemes where companies pay fines based upon CO2 output per unit produced instead of simply paying tax after production occurs, but also investing heavily early stages research projects aimed specifically toward developing alternative sources of power generation capable producing electricity efficiently yet cleanly via solar panels placed strategically throughout urban areas alongside existing infrastructure networks already serving residential neighborhoods near major cities worldwide."
Thirdly, according to Richard Heinberg author most recently published book titled Peak Everything? A Guide To Living Sustainably In An Age Of Limits,"we must recognize reality." He argues that despite claims otherwise human civilization cannot continue indefinitely consuming natural resources at current rates nor emitting vast quantities pollutants causing global warming unless drastic changes occur soonest possible moment available right away!
Fourth point involves recognizing fact humans consume far too much food compared historical norms resulting excessive waste leading environmental degradation especially water scarcity issues affecting millions lives globally every single day!

The first practical photographic medium was created by Joseph Nicephore Niepce around 1816; he used glass plates coated with bitumen ink. The story goes like so: you're some sort of alien who has crash-landed onto Earth after being sent there from your home planet for unknown reasons. You have no memory whatsoever about yourself or how/why you got here; all you know are two things:
1.) Your name - which happens to be 'world' itself!
And 2.) That somewhere nearby lies another world just waiting to be discovered...
So off into space we go! The first thing our hero does upon arriving at his new destination is find himself a ship...which he promptly crashes while trying to land safely back down again. Now stranded without any means of transportation, what else can poor ol' WORLDO do? Well, luckily enough, someone left behind their own spaceship when they went away on vacation last week, complete with everything needed to get him up & running once more. So now armed only with said vessel, along with nothing except basic survival instincts, WORLD sets forth across uncharted territory searching desperately for answers regarding both where exactly HE comes from AND why nobody seems able to remember HIM AT ALL!!!
It’s hard to describe precisely HOW fun “WORLD” actually IS because honestly speaking…there isn’t much gameplay involved beyond exploring different areas within each level until eventually reaching its conclusion via solving puzzles along way…
But trust us – even though most people might dismiss such titles nowadays due lackluster graphics compared modern standards ,this particular gem still manages hold strong appeal thanks largely part nostalgia factor combined great sense humor throughout entire experience . Plus bonus points awarded simply facting title alone already tells plenty backstory than usual fare found elsewhere these days .
In short : If looking something unique yet enjoyable mix classic point n click adventures meets sci fi elements then definitely give ‘em try !
